paragraphs: The day Yao Chang was brought into Chang’an under guard, workers were dismantling the rain-damaged wooden barricade at the western gate.

The gate guards spotted the prison cart from afar. They ordered the workmen back against the wall, produced the escort register, checked its entries against the clay seal on the cart, and counted the five hundred soldiers one by one. Yao Chang sat inside with his wounded leg propped on a straw cushion, his boot unlaced. Rain along the road had rusted the chains red. Yet his wrists were clean, and though he no longer wore an official robe, his hands still went through the old motion of straightening his sleeves.

He recognized the commandant at the gate. On the night of his escape, he had hidden beneath the mats of a cart carrying corpses to the common burial ground. The commandant, newly transferred to the western gate, had once lifted a ragged mat with the tip of his halberd. Now they faced each other across the barrier. After looking at him for a long while, the commandant read from the register: “Yao Chang, formerly Minister of Imperial Sacrifices. Held for trial on charges including raising troops without authority, seizing granaries, and attacking garrisons.”
“You still have my title,” Yao Chang said.
“Your former title.”
“Another inch with that halberd that night, and so many people at Anding might still be alive.”
The commandant returned the register to the escort officer, his face expressionless. “That night my orders were to inspect carts. Today my orders are to deliver a prisoner.”

Yao Chang gazed down the familiar road beyond the gate, and his smile faded. He had expected to be paraded through the streets. The people of Chang’an had reasons enough to throw stones, and the court reasons enough to make him the object of their anger. But the cart avoided Vermilion Bird Avenue, taking a narrow road eastward beneath the walls. A firewood seller recognized him nonetheless, lunged at the cart and shouted about the eleven lives lost at Liugou. The soldiers held the man back, but a clod of mud had already struck Yao Chang’s knee.
“I did not set the fire at Liugou,” Yao Chang said.
Pinned to the ground, the wood seller cried hoarsely, “The man who lit it called you his lord!”
Yao Chang said no more. The cart rolled on; an iron wheel dropped into a rut, and the jolt sent a white flash through his injured leg. He bore it without a sound.

The gate of the Court of Justice prison was low. Once the escort officer surrendered his warrant, the warden summoned a physician before anything else. The physician cut away the rotting bandages around Yao Chang’s leg and picked two grains of sand from the edge of the wound. When the medicine touched raw flesh, Yao Chang clutched the straw mat. On the physician’s wrist he noticed an old arrow scar.
“Which battalion were you with?”
“I served as an army physician at Anding.”
“A Qiang battalion?”
“A mixed battalion. They brought me whoever was hurt. All I asked was where the wound was.”
Yao Chang looked up at him. “That does simplify matters.”
“Keeping still would simplify them further.” The physician tied the fresh dressing firmly. “The Court of Justice has questions for you yet. We cannot let you rot to death in here first.”

The first written deposition reached his cell on the third day. The presiding judge, Han Zheng, was a man in his forties whose cuffs had frayed to fuzz, quite unlike the grand men of Chang’an whom Yao Chang remembered. Han did not begin by denouncing him as a traitor, nor would he let the clerk write, “The criminal has confessed.” He brought seven stacks of records and arranged them by prefecture and county. The first concerned the forged edict and the night of disorder in Chang’an; the second the raising of troops at White Grass Valley; then came the seizure of the Anding granary, the fire at Liugou, the battle at White Horse Slope, and reports of missing people from various districts.
“We shall begin with what can be established,” Han Zheng said.
Yao Chang turned to the note that read, “If Chang’an falls into disorder, the old gates can open.” He recognized the handwriting, and his hand stopped. Han waited for him to speak.
“The writing is mine. I cannot remember whom I sent it to.”
“You remembered last night, but have forgotten today?”
“I have many old friends. Name the wrong one, and I drag another household into this.”
Han had the clerk record his words precisely. Then he asked, “Did you forge the edict?”
“No.”
“When did you learn that someone meant to move against the palace gates?”
“Before I escaped. Someone said the old pattern of the traveling palace’s fish tally might prove useful. I never saw the edict.”
“Why did you not report it?”
Yao Chang leaned against the wall, and pain tightened in his leg. “Because if the gates were thrown into confusion, the men guarding me would have no time for me. I wanted to get away.”
The clerk wrote it down. Han did not use the admission to force a confession that Yao had planned the forgery. Instead he removed the note from the bundle and marked it for separate inquiry.

There were two witnesses in the Liugou case. One was the firewood seller, Xu Lin, whose younger brother had died in a burned house. The other was a supply soldier who had joined Yao’s army. The soldier said Liang’s contingent had first seized grain. When the villagers resisted, unruly troops set the place alight. The following day the contingent’s leader sent Yao Chang captured cattle and horses, and Yao allowed him to keep most of them.
“Did he tell you there had been deaths?” Han asked.
“He did. He gave no number.”
“Did you investigate?”
“The camp at White Grass Valley had only just been formed. Liang brought three thousand men. Had I executed him before the ranks, all three thousand would have dispersed that day.”
Xu Lin, kneeling at the side of the hall, suddenly raised his head. “If they had dispersed, would my brother have lived?”

Yao Chang looked at him. The young man’s face was blackened, and only four fingers protruded from one sleeve. Yao thought of offering one of the explanations men in armies always offered. But when the words reached his throat, they would not come. Xu Lin said, “My brother was afraid of fire. Every night before sleeping he poured water over the ashes in the stove. Your men blocked the door with burning straw. He couldn’t even get over the courtyard wall.”
Han Zheng had a bowl of water brought for Xu Lin. When the man could breathe evenly again, he asked Yao Chang, “You knew of the killing and plunder, yet failed to punish it. What have you to say?”
“Nothing in my defense.”
“Eleven lives cannot be omitted from the record because you needed three thousand soldiers.”
“Record them.” Yao Chang closed his eyes. “Put them in your records.”

Over the next seven days, the prison office struck out two other accusations. One man laid the slaughter of an entire village at Yao’s door, but the relay-station records placed him a hundred li away at the time. A surrendered soldier claimed that Yao had secretly ordered prisoners poisoned; after the graves were reopened, a physician identified signs of epidemic disease. There was, however, clear evidence that Yao had circulated proclamations asserting that the Heavenly King was dead and all Qiang households were to be deported: he had personally stamped the proclamation on the day it was posted. The case against Du Yan of Anding for illegally detaining soldiers' families and the shooting of women by garrison troops also reached the Court of Justice. It had to be kept separate from Yao’s case. One wrong could not be used to cancel another.
When Yao saw Han personally cross out two charges, he asked, “If you remove two, will you spare my life tomorrow?”
“Not necessarily.”
“Then why cross them out?”
Han sharpened his brush tip, dipped it in ink and signed beside the corrections. “The man is here. None of his deeds will run away. Why lend him deeds he never committed?”

Yao Chang studied the small characters. Countless times he had earned merit before Fu Jian, and more than once he had escaped disaster by reading the emperor’s face. Now, for the first time, he met someone who neither demanded a convenient confession nor treated his explanations as favors to be granted.

The grand court in Chang’an did not stop for his sake. Fu Hong continued as regent at the Department of State Affairs, while medical reports came from the traveling palace at Luoyang every third day. Fu Jian drifted in and out of consciousness and still could not travel. Han Zheng submitted the hearing records, testimony and dismissed charges to the Department, asking the crown prince and Fu Rong to authorize a public conclusion. Fu Hong read them and hesitated at the question, “Await the Heavenly King’s personal interrogation?” At last he wrote: Convene the hearing according to law. Send the judgment to Luoyang for review. His Majesty’s illness must not prolong detention indefinitely.

There was no imperial throne at the public hearing. The Court of Justice sat in the center, with one representative each from the censorate, the household office and the Central Army Office. Qiang elders, wounded soldiers and survivors of Liugou were admitted on presentation of their names and warrants. Some sat beyond the threshold; others, unable to kneel steadily, held pillars for support. As Yao Chang entered, nothing could be heard in the hall but the faint rattle of his fetters.

Han read the charges one by one. On the forged edict, Yao stood accused of knowing without reporting, escaping in the confusion, and secretly contacting former subordinates. Who had directed Zhao Qian to carry the false tally to the gate was still under investigation, and was not included among Yao’s proven offenses. On the attacks against garrisons, the registers gave the names of Qin soldiers killed at Anding and the number of surrendered men wounded. At Liugou, Xu Lin held a charred door bar in his hands. He did not weep.
“Are the charges wrongly stated?”
“A few are recorded more clearly than I remember,” Yao Chang said. “I can admit them.”

Han ordered each admission entered separately, then sought a capital sentence for armed rebellion, killing, plunder and the other proven offenses. Fu Hong did not immediately approve it. After reading the Liugou depositions he asked Yao, “Your proclamation said the court would move away every Qiang household. Had you seen such an edict yourself?”
“No.”
“Then why write it?”
“Chang’an had detained their families. Innocent women had been killed. They were frightened. When fear goes deep enough, it needs no further edict.”
“You know Du Yan is being prosecuted in a separate case.”

“When I raised my army, I did not know he would ever face trial.” Yao looked at the crown prince. “You may establish the truth of everything afterward. Those Qiang households had no such time that night.”
Fu Hong made no excuses for Du Yan. He asked only, “If you knew the people were afraid, why did you send them against Anding?”

The chains shifted slightly between Yao’s fingers. He glanced at several former Qiang chieftains standing to the side. After a long silence he said, “Because I wanted to win as well. I promised them pasture, their old camps and three years without levies. If we did not attack the city, those promises would have dissolved the next day.”
The admission left the hall quiet for a long time. The Qiang elders lowered their heads. Xu Lin tightened his grip on the door bar and murmured, “Win what? The lives of a whole village?”

By the time the case papers reached Luoyang, Fu Jian could at last sit up in bed to read. His physicians warned him against exertion, but he went through every page. When he came to an appended statement in which Yao Chang had asked why Qin still belonged to the Fu family, he made Fu Rong read it twice. Yao had raised the question in court; it was not among his capital crimes. Fu Jian listened and laid the paper beside his pillow.
“I never taught him to ask that.”
“He wanted the highest place for himself,” Fu Rong said.
“Yes.” Fu Jian did not defend Yao. “But the point he raised does not vanish merely because he deserves to die.”

Fu Rong waited until his elder brother had recovered from a spell of breathlessness before handing over the verdict. Fu Jian wrote a single character of approval slowly in the place reserved for review, then ordered his seal delivered to the Department of State Affairs and the papers archived in the prescribed order. An edict exempting Yao’s uninvolved relatives from collective punishment went out the same day as the judgment. Former soldiers of Yao’s force who had taken no part in the crimes could return to the household registers according to their individual conduct. Relief for Liugou and the investigation of unlawful confinement at Anding were not to be delayed.

The Court of Justice set the execution for three days later. On the preceding night Yao was permitted a family visit. An elderly clansman, his hair already white, came carrying an old robe neatly mended. He had meant to plead with the court for mercy, but when he saw Yao he asked only, “Is the banner from White Grass Valley still there?”
“Burned.”

The old man sat down in a daze. Looking at the robe in his arms, Yao suddenly remembered his early days, when Di and Qiang troops had camped beside a river and his men had fought over a cooking pot. He had smashed it before them all and declared that every battalion would draw grain together. Back then he had truly believed that if the distribution was fair, everyone would follow him. Years later he had raised his own banner, yet for fear of losing three thousand men he had not dared seek justice for the eleven dead at Liugou.
“When our clan farms its land in years to come,” he told the old man, “do not claim fields in my name.”
The old man lowered his head in assent. Only when he was about to leave did he say, “There will always be children who remember you.”
“Then let them remember what I did,” Yao Chang said. “Do not invent victories for me.”

Before dawn the next day, people gathered outside the prison to watch the execution. Han Zheng read the sentence as prescribed; the three sets of evidence had been sealed and stored separately. Yao listened to the end and merely nodded. “I understand.” The blade flashed. A flock of crows burst from the gate tower, their cries harsh and piercing. Relatives came with a wooden casket to claim his remains. The prison clerks checked their warrant and let them leave by the side gate. His body was not exposed, nor put on display for three days.

That same day Xu Lin went to the ruins of Liugou to make offerings to his brother. The new house had only half a wall, and the timber of the doorway still bore scorch marks. He folded the posted judgment from the Court of Justice and placed it beneath the stove. He did not tell his neighbors that they would sleep peacefully now. He knew that what kept them awake would not end with a single fall of the blade.

In Luoyang Fu Jian received the report of the execution. The first summer heat lay beyond the window; the medicine pot bubbled beside his bed. He did not order Yao Chang’s name erased from the old chronicles, nor command historians to portray himself as a ruler who had always seen through the man. Fu Rong stood nearby as his brother slipped an extra sheet into the case file. It recorded the eleven dead at Liugou, the fallen soldiers at White Horse Slope, and the names of Qiang households wrongfully imprisoned.
“All these people must remain in the record,” Fu Jian said.
Fu Rong asked, “So that Yao Chang may be condemned?”
“So that afterward they do not remember only Yao Chang.”

The file closed. The blood had been washed away from Chang’an prison, but the bluestone before the courtroom, worn into a shallow groove, remained. The next day another farmer imprisoned over a dispute about fields passed across it. He did not know who had died there the day before. All he feared was that the authorities might award his family’s wheat field to his neighbor.
